page.title: Hybrid Event Production Guide
page.description: Learn the first decisions, run‑of‑show structure, rehearsal plan, staffing model and replay workflow for a successful hybrid event.
page.h1: What should you decide first about hybrid event production?
page.definition: Hybrid event production is the coordinated delivery of a live program to both an on‑site audience and a remote stream, covering venue AV, streaming platform, run‑of‑show, speaker rehearsals and backup contingencies. It also aligns registration, moderation, recording and post‑event analytics.
page.quick_answer: Lock the venue AV contract and choose the streaming platform before finalising the agenda; then assign a single show caller to own the run‑of‑show and schedule a full rehearsal on the real platform two to five days before go‑live.

sections.h2: Which platform and venue AV should you lock first?

blocks.p: Choose the streaming platform and confirm the venue AV contract before the agenda is set. The platform decision drives encoder requirements, audience capacity and moderation features, while the venue AV contract fixes camera feeds, audio routing and on‑site monitoring. Confirm that the platform supports simultaneous interpretation, live polling and branded landing pages if those are required.

sections.h2: How do you structure the run‑of‑show and assign owners?

blocks.p: Create a run‑of‑show with eight workstreams, each owned by a single person. This prevents gaps during transitions and gives a clear escalation path. Document each workstream output in a shared tracker so the show caller can verify completion before each cue.

sections.h2: What rehearsal and backup steps reduce live risk?

blocks.p: Run a full rehearsal on the actual platform two to five days before and a technical check sixty minutes before go‑live. The rehearsal validates speaker timing, slide cues and backup stream switching. Record the rehearsal for reference and capture any timing adjustments needed for the live run.

sections.h2: What staffing model fits a simple webinar versus a summit?

blocks.p: A single producer can run a simple webinar while a summit needs a show caller, speaker manager, moderator and platform operator. Match headcount to session count and risk level. For recurring webinars the same producer can repeat the role, reducing onboarding time.

sections.h2: How do you deliver the replay and measure outcomes?

blocks.p: Publish the edited recording within twenty‑four to forty‑eight hours and track attendance, engagement and conversion metrics. West Peek Productions produces virtual, hybrid and webinar events and sets up marketing, content and creative operations. Schedule a post‑event debrief within one week to review metrics and capture lessons for the next cycle.

faq.q: How far in advance should you book the venue and platform?
faq.a: For a summit or conference lock the venue AV and streaming platform six to eight weeks out; for a webinar three to four weeks is sufficient. Early booking secures preferred dates and allows time for speaker rehearsals.

faq.q: What is the typical cost range for a produced hybrid event?
faq.a: Executive summits and hybrid productions generally run from ten thousand to fifty thousand dollars and above, while moderated webinars fall between two thousand five hundred and seven thousand five hundred dollars per production.

faq.q: Who owns the run‑of‑show during the live event?
faq.a: The show caller owns the run‑of‑show and cues every segment; the platform operator manages the stream health and backup switching. Clear ownership avoids timing drift.

faq.q: What tools help coordinate the production timeline?
faq.a: Teams typically use Asana, Monday.com or Airtable for the calendar, Google Docs or Notion for briefs, and HubSpot or GA4 for post‑event reporting. These tools keep every workstream visible.
